title: The starter applies confinement; a policy is mandatory
Two-phase launch: the stage proves, the host accepts, then the command starts
Enforcement is computed from governed effects, never asserted
One private scratch directory in both confined modes; real temp areas are listed
The launcher and the harness home are never writable by what they confine; the tool endpoint is the one thing granted
Windows: one identifier per write root, a journal, consent, and owner commands
SSH: the operator's OpenSSH, one channel, a multiplexer, no stream keys (crypto/tls has no pre-shared-key mode)
The remote helper is the same dsh binary, installed by a command and pinned by digest
A world is one component; a policy is decoded once and resolved where the files are
A lost connection means outcome unknown; reconnect serves new work; receipts close the gap
The confinement is not audited, says so wherever it is shown, and is reviewed before a stable release
Stream multiplexer over the one SSH channel (replaces forwarded Unix sockets and TLS pre-shared keys)
verified: go list -m -json, go mod download -json, LICENSE, mux.go and stream.go read in the module cache, 2026-11-18; alternative github.com/xtaci/smux v1.5.60 (MIT) verified the same way

title: One policy resolver for every enforcing capability
The sandbox launch stage (shared piece)
The sandbox seam: probe, select, prepare, confirm, report
Linux backends: bubblewrap, then Landlock
macOS backend: Seatbelt
Windows backend: restricted token, journalled grants, consent, cleanup and doctor
Network denial, home protection and the tool endpoint inside each backend
The SSH connection, the helper mode and dsh ssh install
The remote world: filesystem, processes, terminals and sandbox over the helper
Remote file watching over the helper
Policy precedence, root validation on every call, session-scoped registrations, scratch in both confined modes
A zero policy is refused, only the resolver can build one, and config decoding is strict
Enforcement table: backend by kernel version by policy by requirement; unknown evidence and custom runners are never full
Launch protocol with a fake stage: every truncation, refusal and failure leaves the command not run
One root derivation feeds the fence and every profile builder; each real path is resolved once per start
Golden profiles for bubblewrap, Landlock and Seatbelt, including network denial, secret mask, endpoint rule and binary overlay
Probe and selection: chain order, all fail gives unavailable, re-probe after repair and after a launch failure
Windows grant journal with a fake access-control API: intent first, rollback, cleanup of own entries only, shared label left
Windows token identifiers equal the start's roots plus scratch; network denial is refused
Multiplexed transport over an in-memory pipe: a stalled stream does not block requests; limits; half-close; no listener
SSH connection lifecycle with a fake ssh process: identity mismatch, loss without replay, reconnect budget, lease and receipt
Filesystem and process provider contract suites pass against the helper; policy decoded once; confinement returned as data
A writable launcher is refused or overlaid; the denial hint never changes exit code or output
A home inside a write root is refused or kept read-only; delegated execution counts against full; exposure never changes the state; helper policies
Remote file watching: events in order, a resync after a dropped connection, no replay
The not-audited statement is shown verbatim in every place, and a stable release needs a recorded review
Import direction: only the starter creates processes, consumers import no backend, the stage imports three sources
Linux: bubblewrap confines, Landlock is the fallback, an old kernel is reported partial
With no usable backend, a confined command does not run (Linux)
macOS Seatbelt confines
Windows restricted token: roots, consent, journal, cleanup
Network denial, home protection and dsh tool call on every backend
A real SSH host: trust, install, remote world, loss and receipts
The policy text does not stop a real model from trying, and escalating, a denied task

reason: The seam vocabulary (three modes, a policy per call, reported enforcement, fail closed) is kept as the Go contract package; the argv-returning confine call becomes a Launch the one process starter applies, and enforcement is computed instead of returned by the provider.

The per-platform backend chain and its profiles are kept (bubblewrap then Landlock, Seatbelt, Windows token); every backend is probed at start, the C launcher and stderr failure rules are replaced by the launch stage and its status channel.

The resolver keeps upstream's precedence, the sandbox/mode session event, effect-scoped extra roots and the model-visible policy section, and gains the network setting, the scratch directory and a required-enforcement field.

The write-restricted Low-integrity token and the three-edit grant are kept and made from typed golang.org/x/sys calls in the host; the runner process and the PowerShell diagnosis skill are replaced by an in-process token build, a grant journal and owner commands.

The remote filesystem provider is kept as a thin forwarder to the helper, which runs the local filesystem provider where the files are; file content moves to its own stream so the 8 MiB frame cap disappears.

Upstream needs a separate provider that asks the helper for a wrapped argv; in Go a remote start runs the same seam on the remote host and returns the confinement as data, so the provider is part of the remote world component.

The OpenSSH alias, batch mode, strict host keys, helper identity check, lease and no-replay rule are kept; the control master, forwarded Unix sockets and TLS pre-shared keys are replaced by one channel with a stream multiplexer, because Go's crypto/tls has no pre-shared-key mode.

The package exists to pack Node, the helper and worker entry points into one executable with loose native files; the Go helper is a hidden mode of the one static dsh binary, so there is no carrier, no resolution hook and no worker dispatch.

The remote process and terminal provider is kept as a forwarder to the helper's local starter; standard streams and terminal bytes are multiplexed streams owned by the process handle instead of forwarded sockets.

The scripts build, inspect and release the Node single-file helper for four targets; the Go release already builds dsh for every target, dsh ssh install uploads and pins it, and the handshake probe survives as the hello check and the real-host scenario.

The Windows backend gives every write root its own capability identifier and builds each start's token with exactly that start's roots, so sandboxed processes honour extra roots like the file tools do.
Hard-link aliases, unconfined reads and trees stamped by another sandbox remain outside what the restricted-token mechanism can govern on Windows.
justification: These are properties of the write-restricted token that upstream chose over AppContainer because AppContainer needs read grants on every path; no unprivileged Windows mechanism removes them. Every start reports partial with the named effects, and a policy that requires full is refused.

reason: An older kernel still governs only the Landlock access kinds it knows, so enforcement there is partial in Go as upstream.
justification: This is a kernel property no user-space design changes. The Go design computes the state per start from the kernel's version and the launch stage's report, names the missing kinds, and refuses when the policy requires full.

reason: The macOS backend still depends on the deprecated sandbox-exec program, as upstream.
justification: No unprivileged successor is known for a command-line program to confine a child on macOS. The backend is probed at every start-up, so removal by Apple shows as unavailable before the first command and confined modes fail closed.

reason: The seam re-probes on an operator command, from the UI and automatically after a launch failure, so installing or repairing a backend takes effect without reloading the component.
A custom runner must run the launch stage as its command, passes the same functional probe and canary as built-in backends, and can never be reported full, so it is no longer an unprobed assertion.

A write-root grant is an effect registered through the agent's scope, so building the agent for a resumed or forked session registers it again without a manual step; authority is still never replayed from the session log.
The Go policy gains a network setting, but still has no knob for process policy.
justification: Process visibility is governed only as a side effect of bubblewrap; no unprivileged mechanism covers it on Linux without bubblewrap, on macOS and on Windows, so a policy knob would read partial almost everywhere. The limit is stated in the specification.

reason: Backends are probed at start, so the backend is known before the first model request and the resolver lists the real scratch and temporary paths in the model-visible section.

Diagnosis and cleanup are compiled-in owner commands: nothing is extracted to disk, and cleanup removes the labels the journal recorded; a missing WRITE_DAC is reported as a precondition only the directory's owner can fix.
A preflight before the consent step refuses a volume that stores no access-control lists and warns on a drive root or profile root; the real-Windows scenario covers a FAT-class volume.
The host, which is unconfined, classifies a preparation failure itself by reading descriptors; repairs are an owner command, so the model never needs to escalate a call to diagnose.
The read-only mode also receives the private scratch directory as its temporary area, so PowerShell can create its probe files and starts in the same language mode as under workspace-write.
There is no sandbox instance to reuse across workspaces: each start's token is built with exactly the identifiers of that start's write roots.

Every access-control change is journalled as intent before it is made, so a start-up sweep and the cleanup command find and remove a scratch directory or entry that a failed cleanup or a crash left behind.
The journal records the volume and file identity of each granted directory, so the cleanup command finds and removes entries on a workspace that was renamed.
The journal stores the original security descriptor before the first change, so revoking restores a directory that had no access list to exactly that state.
A program confined by the Windows token still cannot give its own children named-pipe standard streams.
justification: Windows assigns a new named pipe a default descriptor that no restricting identifier satisfies, and adding the user's own identifier to the token would remove the write restriction. The limit is stated in the model-visible policy text on Windows; inherited and anonymous pipes work.

reason: The first grant on a directory still walks every descendant, because Windows propagates inheritable entries eagerly.
justification: The propagation is operating-system behaviour and the confined child needs the inherited entries and label. The Go design moves the cost to the one-time consent step, with progress and cancellation, so it never runs inside a command's time limit.

reason: The Windows token still restricts writes only; reads are unconfined and sockets cannot be restricted.
justification: WRITE_RESTRICTED intersects write access only and the mechanism has no socket control. Reads are a stated limit on every platform, and a policy with the network denied fails closed on Windows instead of running.

reason: A Low-integrity child still cannot read objects that another AppContainer-based tool stamped with a package identifier.
justification: This is a kernel access rule outside the harness's control. The doctor command names the affected objects and offers the repair to the directory's owner, and the limit is one of the named reasons for partial enforcement.

reason: The Go policy adds a network setting and masks the secret directory where a backend can, but still expresses no process, system-call or device restriction.
justification: No unprivileged mechanism covers process visibility, system calls or devices on all three operating-system families, and a dimension only one backend enforces would be reported partial everywhere else. The limit is stated in the security model.

reason: A world is one component that provides the filesystem, process and sandbox providers together, so a container or remote executor is added as a world and a mismatched trio cannot be mounted; same-world confinement stays the seam's stated scope.
A file-effect denial inside a spawned command is still inferred from the command's stderr.
justification: No backend offers an unprivileged, typed denial report. The Go design keeps one classifier inside the seam, labels its result a hint that never changes the exit code, and gives typed denials for file tools, which run in the host.

reason: Launcher status travels on a private descriptor pair that closes before the command's first instruction, so a confined child cannot forge it and its exit code and output are never read as launcher failure.

The ordered backend chain is inside the one seam, and a world's providers mounted in one agent's scope serve that agent only, so a local and a remote sandbox coexist in one host without separate trees.
File content travels on its own multiplexed stream instead of inside a JSON message, so a whole-file read is not bounded by the message size limit.
The helper runs the shared watch package on the remote host and streams change events to the host, so the remote filesystem provider supports watching.
The server-rendered UI never dereferences a file address itself: a host route reads through the filesystem seam of the session's world, so a remote file is shown or downloaded like a local one.
Remote confinement still does not restrict process visibility, and a remote backend that is partial stays partial.
justification: The remote host runs the same backends with the same limits as a local host; the network setting is enforced remotely, but process visibility and partial kernels are properties of the remote operating system. The remote confinement state is reported on every result.

reason: The SSH host and the installed helper are still trusted infrastructure in the Go design.
justification: The remote machine executes every file and process request it is sent, so no client-side design makes a hostile host safe; the digest check only detects a wrong or stale helper. The trust statement is shown at connect and in the documentation.

reason: The helper is the statically linked dsh binary built for every released target with cgo off, so there is no glibc or musl split and a Windows binary exists; a Windows remote endpoint is a P2 part of the remote world.
The dsh ssh install command uploads the binary over the operator's ssh, verifies it and pins its digest in the writable config layer, and the connection state is a seam fact the UI can show.
The limit exists only because upstream's helper executable embeds a Node runtime that users might mistake for a general Node command; the Go helper embeds no interpreter.

The transport needs no control master or socket forwarding, so a Windows machine can be the local end; provisioning is one command; the connection fiber reconnects for new work under a budget. Replay stays forbidden by decision, not by omission.
UI file and workspace views are host routes that read through the filesystem seam of the session's world, so they work for a remote world without assuming host paths.

There are no per-stream keys to steal because streams are multiplexed inside the one SSH channel, and the helper marks itself non-dumpable and refuses debugger attachment; the remaining trust in the remote host is recorded as a carried limit.

Spill files live in the helper's lock-held runtime directory and are removed at close, at lease expiry, or by the next helper's start-up sweep, so they no longer wait for external temporary-file cleanup.
Each output stream belongs to its process handle and is closed with the handle or its context, and an unread stream stalls only its own sender through its own flow-control window.

The helper writes a cleanup receipt when lease-expiry cleanup ends, and the next connection reads the receipts of lost instances and logs them, so remote termination can be confirmed after a reconnect; until then the log says outcome unknown.

Replaced by the Go struct local.Config (probe and launch time limits, an optional reduced backend chain, an optional custom runner); runnerFailureSignatures has no successor because launcher status is out of band.
Replaced by the Go struct policy.Config (default mode read-only, fallback root, extra write roots) with two added fields, the network setting and the required enforcement level.

Replaced by the Go struct ssh.Config (alias, helper path and digest, workspace, request time limit, message and pending limits, lease, reconnect budget); the launch kind is gone because there is one helper kind.

ctx.sandbox becomes the service key sandbox.Key with the interface sandbox.Service (Describe, Reprobe, Prepare); Prepare returns a launch plan that the one process starter requires and executes, instead of an argv each consumer spawns and classifies.
ctx.sandboxPolicy becomes the service key policy.Key with the interface policy.Resolver (Resolve, Escalate, ForPlugin, GrantRoot, SetMode), the only constructor of a policy value.

ctx.ssh becomes the service key ssh.Key with the interface ssh.Connection, which reports connection state; its component mounts the filesystem, process and sandbox providers of the remote world together, and request and stream calls are internal to it.

Kept: an operator-owned OpenSSH alias, an installed helper that runs local providers on the remote host, a lease, and no replay after loss. Changed: forwarded sockets and TLS pre-shared keys are replaced by a multiplexer over the one channel, and the helper is the dsh binary.

Kept as decided: an extra write root is an effect owned by the registering component for one live session, is never restored from history, does not revoke what a running process started with, and an invalid path stops the call.

Reversed: the Go host builds the Windows token per start, so each write root carries its own identifier and processes honour extra roots; the journal supplies the grant bookkeeping whose cost made upstream defer this.

Kept: a write-restricted token with capability identifiers instead of AppContainer or mxc, for the same reason (arbitrary reads without read grants). The mechanism is Windows calls reachable from Go without cgo; the runner process is replaced by an in-host token build.

Kept exactly: each grant applies the allow entry, the container-only deny of delete-child and the Low label in one call, and the token is lowered to Low; the real-Windows scenario repeats the delete-escape cases.
Adopted: a policy crosses the wire as one typed message that the helper decodes once and passes on as a Go value.
Adopted: the world that owns the files resolves each root's real path once per start in the one root-derivation function, while extra roots are still re-checked on every start.
